tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). - The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

```
# m-41 hello
- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
```

````

https://github.com/winksaville/def/blob/0123456789ab/TODO.md#feat-the-cycle.

## What changed

- one thing
- another, with the command that shows it:

  ```
  vc-x1 validate --fast
  ```
````

`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times

  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

# vc-x1 config file

Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.

The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
the system. The [vc-config.md](vc-config.md) contains the documentation for the
various toml tables used for configuration and it is also used during compilation to define
the valid contents of this file.

The file [vc-config-model.md](vc-config-model.md) is the model: every table and key a workspace
config may carry, each with its default or a typical value. It is generated from the schema, so it
cannot fall behind the keys the binary knows.

The two repos
- work [[1]]
- agent [[2]]
```toml
[repos]
work = "."
agent = ".agent-session"
```

The agent-repo's name on its remote, which clone and sync need when there is no agent-repo yet to
ask
- agent-repo [[9]]
```toml
[remote]
agent-repo = "vc-x1.agent-session"
```

The agent-file family this repo belongs to: its member name and the sibling repos it answers to
- member [[3]]
- template [[4]]
- messages [[5]]
```toml
[family]
member = "vc-x1"
template = "../vc-x1-template/work"
messages = "../vc-x1-messages"
```

The validation commands, each element one invocation, run in order by `vc-x1 validate`
- full [[6]]
- fast [[7]], `cargo test --bins` alone, the schema's example, wink's call 2026-10-20: the full
  list with plain `cargo test` measured the same 8 s as full, since the fourteen `dr1_*` fixture
  tests cost nothing once the fixture is built, so the only fast worth having skips fmt, clippy,
  the integration tests, and the install. Its trial of 2026-09-21 found a rung's failures in what
  it skips, so a rung's review still runs full
- full checks the source and makes no build to run, wink's call 2026-10-21: the dev build is
  `[build] dev` below, which `vc-x1 run-dev` runs first, so what runs is always the current code,
  and the test build full leaves is what the dev build then reuses
```toml
[validate]
full = [
  "cargo fmt",
  "cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings",
  "cargo test -- --include-ignored",
]
fast = ["cargo test --bins"]
```

The build commands, each element one invocation, run in order, each a plain `cargo build` that
leaves its binary in `target/`, so nothing on the PATH is replaced until `vc-x1 install` copies the
release build there at Land, and both `--locked` so the two builds compile the same dependencies
- release [[10]], the release build, run by `vc-x1 build` so it can be run by `vc-x1 run` before
  `vc-x1 install` copies it at a cycle's Land
- release-bin [[13]], the binary the release build leaves, which `vc-x1 install` copies
- dev [[11]], the dev build, run by `vc-x1 build-dev` and first by `vc-x1 run-dev`, a debug
  build, wink's call 2026-10-21: after full's `cargo test` it reuses the test build and takes
  under a second against a release build's ten, forty against ten when cold, and its overflow
  checks and `debug_assert!` suit a build that exists to be tested. The release profile is then
  built only by `vc-x1 build`
- dev-bin [[12]], the binary the dev build leaves, run by `vc-x1 run-dev` and copied by `vc-x1
  install-dev`
```toml
[build]
release = ["cargo build --release --locked"]
release-bin = "target/release/vc-x1"
dev = ["cargo build --locked"]
dev-bin = "target/debug/vc-x1"
```

The installs, in `[build]`'s order, each list written out so the config says what `vc-x1 install`
and `vc-x1 install-dev` do. Each copies the binary to a `.new` file and then moves it into place,
since a copy onto a running binary fails and a move swaps it in whole, so a copy already running
keeps the old code and the next run gets the new. The lists use `{table.key}` placeholders, filled
with the keys' values, so each path is written once, and `~` is expanded to the home directory, so
the values fit every machine.
- release [[16]], the release install at a cycle's Land, into `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1`
- release-dir [[14]], where it goes
- dev [[17]], the dev install mid-cycle, into `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev`
- dev-dir [[15]], where it goes
- dev-suffix [[18]], what the dev build's file name gets, so it sits beside the release and never
  replaces it
```toml
[install]
release = [
  "cp {build.release-bin} {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new",
  "mv {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new {install.release-dir}/vc-x1",
]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev = [
  "cp {build.dev-bin} {install.dev-dir}/vc-x1{install.dev-suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dev-dir}/vc-x1{install.dev-suffix}.new {install.dev-dir}/vc-x1{install.dev-suffix}",
]
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev-suffix = "-dev"
```

The closing commit's default body, `{title}` the cycle title read from the opening, so `vc-x1
commit --closing` needs no `--body` for a closing that says only where its record is
- body [[19]]
```toml
[closing]
body = 'Closes the cycle "{title}". See details in zCLOSED.md.'
```

The cycle's record files, so `vc-x1 commit --closing` moves the In Progress block from the doing
file into the closed file
- doing [[20]]
- closed [[21]]
```toml
[record]
doing = "zDOING.md"
closed = "zCLOSED.md"
```

The acceptance-test fixtures, one dual workspace per name under the directory, inside the
workspace and gitignored, so a fresh clone builds or fetches its own there and the committed config
names no path on one machine
- fixtures [[8]]
```toml
[test]
fixtures = ".fixtures"
```

[2]: vc-config.md#reposagent
[3]: vc-config.md#familymember
[4]: vc-config.md#familytemplate
[5]: vc-config.md#familymessages
[6]: vc-config.md#validatefull
[7]: vc-config.md#validatefast
[8]: vc-config.md#testfixtures
[9]: vc-config.md#remoteagent-repo
[10]: vc-config.md#buildrelease
[11]: vc-config.md#builddev
[12]: vc-config.md#builddev-bin
[13]: vc-config.md#buildrelease-bin
[14]: vc-config.md#installrelease-dir
[15]: vc-config.md#installdev-dir
[16]: vc-config.md#installrelease
[17]: vc-config.md#installdev
[18]: vc-config.md#installdev-suffix
[19]: vc-config.md#closingbody
[20]: vc-config.md#recorddoing
[21]: vc-config.md#recordclosed

call. Single-step, turned from a ladder at the opening's review, nothing yet pushed.

#### Problem

`AGENTS.md > Working practices` forbids masking a command's exit status and bundling unrelated
commands into one invocation, and the agent broke both through the session of 2026-10-26, a
trailing `; echo rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}` on `sync`, `validate`, `install-dev`, and the pushes, and
again at the acquaint of 2026-10-27, three invocations joined by `;`. Nothing fails when it slips,
so the habit holds until the user catches it, and neither rule is in the Rules index, where the
rules an agent reads as hard are listed. `bash-allow.sh`, the user's `PreToolUse` hook, allows any
command starting `cargo`, `jj`, or `vc-x1`, so a masked `cargo test` runs with no prompt.

#### Solution

What was done:

- `agent-data/bash-guard.sh`, a `PreToolUse` hook on Bash, two text matches on the command and no
  parsing, each a deny whose reason is the rule's form:

  - a `cargo` or `vc-x1` command, by any path and `vc-x1-dev` included, piped into `tail`, `head`,
    `grep`, or `rg`, with no `pipefail` in the command
  - Matching hooks run in parallel and the strictest decision wins, so it overrides
    `bash-allow.sh`'s `allow`.

  `agent-data/inhibit-sleep.sh`, copied verbatim from `~/.claude/hooks/`, and
  `agent-data/hooks.sh`:

    `~/.claude/settings.json`, else what is missing, different, or unregistered, exit 1

  - `test`: `bash-guard.sh` over thirteen commands it must deny or allow

    piped, the `|| { rc=$?; ... }` form kept for reporting.

input.description: Show vc-x1 commit help

content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.12+aab50c7d4082

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, and push it
in the same invocation, as `vc-x1 push` would.

The diff and the description are reviewed before the commit, so the
push publishes what was reviewed. --no-push keeps the commit local,
for a look at it by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` before `vc-x1 push`, and
`[commit] push = false` makes that the default, --push overriding it.

REV is the commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed
as the working copy, else `@-` or any draft below it, described in
place with no new commit and its trailer stamped, so a commit made by
hand becomes a rung's. A draft below `@-` is kept local, since push
publishes `@-`.

--closing <BM|REV> closes the cycle whose tip it names, onto the trunk,
--land's or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent: one commit above the
trunk is finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of
the trunk and the tip. A tip that is not @- is closed by a detour, @
moving onto it and returning after. --land [TRUNK] lands it: the trunk
fast-forwarded and pushed and the closing's bookmark deleted, every
check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

Usage: vc-x1 commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE> [REV]

Arguments:
  [REV]
          The commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed as the
          working copy; `@-` or any draft below it is described in place with no
          new commit, its trailer stamped, so a commit made by hand becomes a
          rung's. Not with `--opening` or `--closing`

Options:
  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or either repo,
          or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --title <STR>
          Commit title, the Conventional Commit line; with `--opening` or
          `--closing` the bare cycle title [default with `--closing`: read from
          the opening]

      --body <STR|@PATH>
          Commit body, the problem and its solutions, or @PATH to read it from a
          file [default with `--closing`: `[closing] body`, or the opening's for
          a single-step cycle]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --closing <BM|REV>
          Close the cycle whose tip this names, a bookmark or a revision, onto
          the trunk, `--land`'s or `[cycle] trunk`: one commit above it is
          finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of the
          trunk and the tip

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --dead-end
          With `--closing`, close the cycle as a dead end: the title ends "
          dead-end closing", always on a closing commit

      --opening [<BOOKMARK>]
          Make the work commit the cycle's opening: " opening" is appended to
          the bare cycle title, and BOOKMARK is created at the work `@-` and
          pushed to `origin` [default: the bare title's slug]

      --skip <SIDE>
          With `--opening`, what it leaves out: `local`, the bookmark is already
          at the work `@-` and is pushed; `remote`, it is created and not
          pushed; `both`, it is only checked. With `--land`, which side of the
          cycle's bookmark is kept: `local`, `remote`, or `both`, none deleted

          Possible values:
          - local:  The bookmark exists at the work `@-` already, so it is not
            created, only pushed
          - remote: The bookmark is created and not pushed
          - both:   The bookmark exists and is neither created nor pushed

      --land [<TRUNK>]
          With `--closing`, land the cycle on TRUNK, the closing's first parent:
          fast-forward it to the closing, push it, and delete the cycle's
          bookmark [default: `[cycle] trunk`, else `main`]

      --bookmark <NAME>
          The bookmark to advance to the work commit, locally, any on the work
          commit's line, at or below it [default: the line's nearest, or
          `--opening`'s]

      --no-advance
          Leave the line's bookmark where it is, rather than advancing it to the
          work commit

      --push
          Push what was committed, over `[commit] push = false`

      --no-push
          Keep the commit local, over `[commit] push`, true when absent

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

input.description: Show vc-x1 merge help

content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.12+aab50c7d4082

Add the sources named to one target commit's parents, after the ones
it has, keeping the target's own change, description, and change id,
so its trailer stays right. The target's tree becomes the merge of
all its parents with its own change applied, `jj rebase -r <target>
-o <p1> ... -o <s1> ...`.

One target, empty or not, and N sources, each --from a revset of one
or more commits, added oldest first: a bookmark, main, a change id,
an earlier merge, a root. A source already a parent is skipped, and
merging one at a time or all at once gives the same tree. `jj undo`
takes a merge back.

-s is required: `w` the work repo or `p` a plain repo, the agent
repo never holding a merge. Refused: a source at or below the target
and a target in jj's immutable(), unless --ignore-immutable.
Reported: a conflicted result.

Usage: vc-x1 merge [OPTIONS] --target <REV> --from <REVSET> --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
      --target <REV>
          The commit whose parents grow, any commit, typically @

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --from <REVSET>
          A source, a revset of one or more commits added to the target's
          parents in the order given; repeat for more

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --ignore-immutable
          Merge into a target in jj's `immutable()`, as `jj` allows it

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s w`, or the repo itself for `-s
          p` [default: the current directory]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repo, required: `w|work` the work repo, or `p|por` a plain repo.
          `a` and `b` are refused, since the agent repo never holds a merge
          
          [possible values: work, por]

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

input.description: Show vc-x1 land help

content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.12+aab50c7d4082

Land a cycle whose last commit is already made: --onto fast-forwarded
to --source and pushed, and the cycle's bookmark deleted locally and
on `origin`, every check made before anything moves. `commit
--closing ... --land` lands the same way, the closing made first.

--source is a bookmark, the cycle's, or a revision, whose current
bookmark, else its nearest parent's above --onto, is the cycle's,
several refused with the list. Left out, it is the one local
bookmark besides --onto. --onto is a local bookmark at its
`origin` position that --source descends from, so a bushy tree lands
anywhere, and Land only fast-forwards: a merge is `commit
--closing`'s. --skip keeps a side of the cycle's bookmark, `local`,
`remote`, or `both`, and --delete-intermediate-bookmarks deletes the
bookmarks strictly between --onto and --source too. --dry-run makes
every check and says each step.

-s is required: `b` a dual workspace, the agent `main` published
with the trunk, and `p` a plain repo. `w` alone could publish
trailers naming agent commits not yet published, and `a` alone has
no cycle to land, so both are refused. The install stays `vc-x1
install`, after.

Usage: vc-x1 land [OPTIONS] --onto <BOOKMARK> --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
      --source <BM|REV>
          The cycle's last commit: a bookmark, the cycle's, or a revision, whose
          current bookmark, else its nearest parent's above `--onto`, is the
          cycle's [default: the one local bookmark besides `--onto`]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --onto <BOOKMARK>
          The bookmark landed on, fast-forwarded to `--source`: a local bookmark
          at its `origin` position that `--source` descends from

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --skip <SIDE>
          Which side of the cycle's bookmark is kept: `local`, `remote`, or
          `both`, none deleted

      --delete-intermediate-bookmarks
          Also delete the bookmarks on the commits strictly between `--onto` and
          `--source`, locally and on origin, as `--skip` allows: a stack of
          cycles landing together [default: named as merged and kept]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b`, or the repo itself for `-s
          p` [default: the current directory]

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `b|both` a dual workspace, or `p|por` a plain
          repo. `w` alone is refused, since it could publish trailers naming
          agent commits not yet published, and `a` alone, which has no cycle to
          land
          
          [possible values: both, por]

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

108	
109	`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
110	and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
111	of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
112	([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
113	repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:
114	
115	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
116	  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
117	  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
118	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
119	  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
120	  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` by hand is the rest of it.
121	- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
122	  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
123	- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
124	  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
125	    bookmark the work-repo is on.
126	  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
127	    the wrong remote ref.
128	- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
129	  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
130	    the squash.
131	  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
132	  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
133	
134	A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
135	re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
136	
137	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
138	
139	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
140	coordinating with everyone involved first**
141	([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
142	and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
143	described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
144	covered. That is a [local
145	ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.
146	
147	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
148	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
149	stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
150	`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.
151	
152	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
153	
154	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
155	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
156	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
157	
158	**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
159	algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
160	and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
161	
162	- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
163	  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
164	- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
165	  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
166	  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
167	- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
168	  ready to be seen.
169	
170	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent, begun by a
171	sync that found `main` unmoved ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)). Every
172	`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
173	stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
174	closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
175	rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
176	
177	1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
178	   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
179	   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
180	   (`@` sits directly above it).
181	2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
182	   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
183	   as it is.
184	3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
185	   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
186	4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
187	   cycle anymore.
188	5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
189	   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
190	   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
191	   disposal once fully merged.
192	
193	- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
194	  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
195	- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
196	  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
197	
198	**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
199	bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):
200	
201	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
202	  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
203	  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
204	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
205	- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
206	  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
207	
208	## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
209	
210	A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
211	carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
212	holder.
213	
214	- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
215	- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
216	- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
217	  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
218	- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
219	  locally and remotely
220	
221	The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
222	freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
223	one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
224	rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.
225	
226	## Close-out shapes
227	
228	The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
229	[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
230	is one commit and lands as it is:
231	
232	- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
233	  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
234	  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
235	  by the landing fast-forward itself.
236	- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.
237	
238	Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
239	rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
240	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
241	
242	**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
243	whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
244	described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
245	trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
246	and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.
247	
248	## Read a change in gitk at full context
249	
250	gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
251	"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
252	is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:
253	
254	- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
255	  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
256	- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
257	  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
258	- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
259	  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.
260	
261	The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
262	together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:
263	
264	- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
265	- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".
266	
267	Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`.
268	If `<base>` is the parent of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing`, that is the cycle's
269	net change, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).
270	
271	## Trapezoid close-out recipe
272	
273	The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
274	close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
275	trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
276	with Land's fast-forward.
277	
278	```
279	  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
280	                      \                    /
281	  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
282	```
283	
284	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
285	  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
286	  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
287	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
288	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.
289	
290	1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
291	   order is the argument order.
292	2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
293	   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
294	   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
295	   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
296	3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
297	   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
298	   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
299	   `jj log --no-graph`.
300	
301	Details:
302	
303	- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
304	  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
305	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
306	  fast-forward.
307	
308	Recovery:
309	
310	- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
311	  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
312	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
313	  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
314	  recovery is forward-only.
315	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
316	  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.
317	
318	## Local ladders
319	
320	The jj moves behind [Local ladders](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders), a rung's scratch chain of commits
321	that never leaves the machine. Ladder commits are scratch, for review and bisection only. Per ladder
322	commit:
323	
324	1. `jj new -R .`: a fresh empty `@`.
325	2. Do the commit's work.
326	3. `vc-x1 validate --fast` (the `[validate] fast` table). Non-negotiable.
327	4. `jj describe -m "..." -R .`: a scratch working title. This first-time authoring is the one
328	   permitted describe.
329	
330	At the end, squash the chain into the rung (below) and continue the per-rung flow from its
331	validation step. `vc-x1 push` then publishes the single commit and stamps its one `ochid:`. A
332	sub-cycle that deserves its own record nests the version suffix
333	([versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)) and names its rungs like any other.
334	
335	Navigating:
336	
337	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: the whole ladder from its base.
338	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder commit by chid prefix, for bisection.
339	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
340	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in isolation.
341	
342	Modifying any ladder commit rewrites it in place, and descendants auto-rebase.
343	
344	The squash, `jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`, takes `<base>` as the parent of the
345	first ladder commit, and `-u` keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'. After it, history
346	is linear (`<base> -> @`) and the intermediate commits are auto-abandoned. For N = 1 the range is
347	empty and the squash is a no-op.
348	
349	Recovery:
350	
351	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .` drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the
352	  same parent.
353	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`, make corrections, then
354	  `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>` to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
355	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows the op history, and
356	  `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts to that point. Full undo, so only to start over.
357	
358	## Resolvability
